Replacing worn turf on ChampionsGate's oldest sections

Turf removal and replacement in ChampionsGate is priced per job rather than off a table, based on how much of the old base can be reused. The community's roots go back to 1998, which puts its earliest sections and any first-generation synthetic turf installed there well into the age range where a base correction, not just a new surface, becomes the real scope of work.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

A community old enough for its first turf generation to be aging out

ChampionsGate's Community Development District dates to 1998 (per the district’s own site), which means any synthetic turf installed in the community's earliest phase is now well past the 10 to 20 year lifespan a well-built system typically reaches, depending on UV stabilization and traffic. A replacement job on one of these older lots often starts with a base inspection rather than an assumption that the original crushed rock is still doing its job, since two decades of settling changes what's underneath more than the worn-out surface on top suggests.

Flatwoods soil settles differently than ridge sand over twenty years

On the Osceola side of ChampionsGate, where flatwoods soils such as Immokalee sit under a seasonally high water table, a base that was fine at installation can settle unevenly after years of wet-season saturation, which shows up as a soft or uneven spot once the old turf comes up. On the Polk-side ridge, where Candler sand drains excessively rather than holding water, the more common issue at replacement is a base that's washed thin in spots rather than one that's settled soft. Both call for regrading before new turf goes down, just for opposite reasons.

A base that looks flat but was never washed to begin with

An older ChampionsGate lawn's base can appear level and well-compacted on the surface while still holding a fines crust from subgrade material that was never washed before the original install, years before the current standard required it. That crust doesn't announce itself as a problem until the turf above it is pulled up during a replacement, at which point it's clear the base was never actually draining the way it looked like it was. Flat isn't the same as functional, which is why we check for a crust, not just for slope, before deciding a base can stay.

Staging demo so old debris doesn't contaminate a kept base

When part of a ChampionsGate lawn's base is solid enough to reuse, the old turf and infill coming out of the rest of the yard get staged and hauled away in a way that keeps loose material from falling back into the section being kept. Skipping this staging step risks mixing years-old, possibly crusted infill back into a base that was otherwise fine, undoing the reason for keeping it in the first place. This sequencing matters more on a replacement than a first-time install, since there's old material moving through the site that a new-build job never has to manage.

Say you have 1,100 sq ft of turf installed in ChampionsGate's early years

Say you have 1,100 sq ft of turf installed in one of ChampionsGate's earliest sections not long after the community's 1998 start, now faded, thin in the high-traffic paths, and showing a soft spot near where an old sprinkler head sits underneath. At $8–$18 per sq ft, replacement runs $8,800 to $19,800, with the final number depending heavily on whether the base needs a full regrade or just a fresh compacted lift on top of what's still sound. Confirming that old irrigation head is properly capped, not just covered, is a small addition to the job that closes out a two-decade-old shortcut before new turf goes back down on top of it.

Choosing a PFAS-free product during a replacement

Florida's turf standard bars intentionally added PFAS in any new synthetic turf installation, and a ChampionsGate homeowner replacing an older lawn gets to choose from current product lines built to that standard rather than whatever was on the market when the original turf went in. Asking a supplier for documentation on this point during a replacement is a reasonable ask, since it's exactly the kind of material change a full re-turf is positioned to address that a smaller repair job never would be.

What changed in the rules since the original install

A lot turfed years before May 2026 was built under whatever standard existed at the time, which in most of Osceola and Polk County meant no published local turf rule at all. A replacement project today has to meet the current state standard regardless of what the original installation used, which most often means confirming the infill is a compliant natural material and that any irrigation heads under the old turf were actually capped rather than just buried, since older installs sometimes skipped that step. Our piece on turf lifespan in Florida sets expectations for a new system, and our ChampionsGate area page has the rest of the community's local rules in one place, alongside neighboring Reunion.

An irrigation line capped with tape instead of properly sealed

A sprinkler line simply folded over and taped rather than cut back and capped with a proper fitting is a common shortcut on a ChampionsGate replacement, and tape doesn't hold against water pressure the way a sealed cap does. A line that fails this way months later can undermine the new base from below with a slow, hidden leak, the kind of problem that's invisible until a soft spot appears in turf that's only been down a short time. Confirming each line was properly capped, not just covered, is worth asking about directly.

Watching a corrected footprint for a new drainage low point

Moving a ChampionsGate lawn's edge outside a live oak's drip line or farther back from a setback line during replacement changes where water moves across that section of yard, even when the correction itself was overdue and necessary. The boundary where the new, adjusted footprint meets the older, unchanged part of the lawn is worth watching through the first few storms, since a grade change at that line can create a small low point that wasn't there under the old layout until the new one settles in fully.

Questions people ask

Does turf from ChampionsGate's original 1998-era construction need full base replacement?

Not always, but it's worth checking rather than assuming. Two decades of settling affects flatwoods and ridge-sand lots differently, and a base inspection before quoting tells us whether a full regrade is needed or just a refresh.

Do I need to redo the HOA approval for a replacement, or just the original permit?

Most village boards want a fresh submittal for a replacement project even if the original installation was approved years ago, since the board reviewing it today may not be the same one that approved it originally.
